journey_classification.reason: core/orchestrator.ts:52 pins model 'gemini-1.5-flash', which Google shut down on 2025-09-29; every request returns 404. Observed offline behaviour: POST /api/chat -> 500 SECURE_GATEWAY_FAILURE (no-key path). The keyed success path cannot be executed here (egress to generativelanguage.googleapis.com is blocked); the 404 conclusion rests on Google's published changelog.
POST /api/keys/validate pings the same retired model, so validateKey() always returns false; KeyDeck.tsx:37 hard-gates the save on data.valid, so a valid key can never be deployed through the UI.
tests/api.test.ts create/list/delete knowledge entries against the real server; 57/57 pass.
GET /api/skills + POST /api/skills/inject exercised end-to-end; live smoke returned {"skills":["System_Info"]}.
tests/api.test.ts proves per-session isolation of the instruction.
tests/purge.test.ts drives audit -> execute -> re-audit against a fixture copy. Functionally correct; the security defect is scored under D3, not D1, per the user-visible-consequence tie-break.
GET /api/tasks/history returned the rolling buffer in the production smoke test.

No browser, no Google account and no Firebase session available in the sandbox. Verified by static reading only: signInWithPopup flow, 8 scopes, 4 window.confirm gates on destructive actions, Bearer token attached to 13 direct googleapis.com fetch calls.
npm run build exit 0; NODE_ENV=production node dist/server.cjs served GET / -> 200 text/html and all API routes on port 3131.

findings.title: Unauthenticated POST /api/purge/execute writes to any path via ../ traversal
findings.impact: Any client that can reach the port can rewrite arbitrary lines of arbitrary existing files on the host filesystem — outside the project root. Concretely demonstrated: a file under /tmp was modified. The same primitive corrupts package.json, .env, tsconfig.json, source files, or any config the process user can write, giving an unauthenticated attacker a code-modification foothold that becomes RCE on the next build/run.
findings.exploit_or_repro: curl -X POST http://host:3000/api/purge/execute -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"items":[{"file":"../../../<abs-path-rel-to-cwd>","line":<N>,"text":"<exact trimmed line>","category":"MOCK_STATIC_DATA"}]}' -> 200 {"status":"success"} and the target line is prefixed with '// DEPLOYED PROSTHETIC CHIP // '. Executed in this session against a file outside the repository root; exit code 0.
findings.remediation: In server.ts /api/purge/execute: (1) reject any item whose resolved path escapes a fixed project root using path.resolve + a path.relative prefix check; (2) restrict writes to an allowlist of extensions (.ts/.tsx) inside <root>/src; (3) require items to originate from a fresh server-side audit rather than trusting client-supplied file/line/text; (4) gate the route behind authentication.

findings.title: Agent pins gemini-1.5-flash, retired by Google 2025-09-29 — every call 404s
findings.impact: The single core value proposition — talking to the agent — cannot succeed with any key. Google's Gemini API changelog records that gemini-1.5-pro, gemini-1.5-flash-8b and gemini-1.5-flash were shut down on 29 September 2025; Google's model documentation states all Gemini 1.0 and 1.5 models are already shut down and every request to them returns a 404 error. Today is 2026-10-05, so the pinned model has been dead for over a year. J1 (chat) and J2 (key deployment, which pings the same model) are both non-functional.
findings.exploit_or_repro: NONE_FOUND locally — outbound TLS to generativelanguage.googleapis.com is blocked in this sandbox (ECONNRESET before handshake, observed in the npm test stderr trace), so the 404 could not be reproduced by execution. The conclusion is drawn from Google's published lifecycle documentation, which is why this finding is graded C rather than A.
findings.remediation: In core/orchestrator.ts, replace both hardcoded 'gemini-1.5-flash' strings (lines 31 and 52) with a supported model read from a single constant/env var (e.g. GEMINI_MODEL, defaulting to a current Flash model). Add a test that asserts no retired model identifier appears in the provider surface.

findings.title: All 14 API routes are unauthenticated, including the destructive purge route
findings.impact: express.json() at server.ts:18 is the only middleware on the app; no session, token, origin or CSRF check exists on any route, and the listener binds 0.0.0.0 (server.ts:303). Anyone on the network can read/modify the knowledge vault, overwrite session protocols, inject skills that reshape agent behaviour, deploy an attacker-controlled Gemini key, and invoke the file-rewriting purge route. The README discloses the gap and instructs operators to run behind a trusted proxy, which reduces but does not remove the risk: nothing in the code enforces that assumption.
findings.exploit_or_repro: curl -X POST http://<host>:3000/api/keys/save -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"key":"<attacker-key>"}' succeeds with no credentials; GET /api/knowledge returns every stored entry with no credentials. Both confirmed by the executed test suite and smoke tests.
findings.remediation: Add a single auth middleware in server.ts guarding every /api route (shared-secret header or a signed session cookie), fail closed with 401, and make it mandatory unless an explicit ALLOW_INSECURE_LOCAL=true escape hatch is set. Add tests asserting 401 without credentials on each route.

findings.title: Tool-call turn is never recorded, so the Gemini function-calling contract is broken
findings.impact: When the provider returns function calls, the engine executes them and appends only the results (engine.ts:49). The assistant turn that carried the functionCall parts is never written to memory, and the orchestrator flattens tool messages into plain user turns prefixed 'TOOL_RESULT [name]:' (orchestrator.ts:44). Gemini's function-calling protocol expects the model's functionCall turn to precede the function responses; here the structured contract is silently replaced by unstructured text. Multi-step tool use therefore degrades to prompt-scraping, tool results cannot be correlated to the call that produced them, and the loop's tool-calling behaviour is untestable against the real provider.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of the loop plus the message-translation map. tests/engine.test.ts uses a StubOrchestrator and never asserts that the functionCall turn is replayed, so the suite cannot catch this.
findings.remediation: In core/engine.ts, record the assistant turn with its tool_calls before appending results (memory.add('assistant', response.content, { tool_calls: response.tool_calls })). In core/orchestrator.ts, map assistant tool_calls to Gemini functionCall parts and tool messages to functionResponse parts instead of flattening both to user text. Add an engine test asserting the replayed history contains the model turn before the tool turn.

findings.title: No LICENSE file — default all-rights-reserved blocks any redistribution
findings.impact: git ls-files returns no LICENSE/COPYING/NOTICE file. Under default copyright law, absence of a licence means no one may legally copy, modify or redistribute the code — including contributors and any downstream deployer. The repository is public on GitHub and also vendors third-party dependencies whose own licences impose attribution duties. The README itself states 'There is no license file in this repository — resolve licensing before redistributing.'
findings.exploit_or_repro: git ls-files | grep -iE 'licen[cs]e|copying|notice' -> no match, exit code 1.
findings.remediation: Choose and add a LICENSE file (MIT/Apache-2.0 are the low-friction options), plus a NOTICE if Apache-2.0. Requires an owner decision — cannot be made autonomously.

findings.title: No CI pipeline — lint, tests, build and verifiers are never enforced
findings.impact: The repository has no .github directory at all (ls .github -> No such file or directory). The five green checks the README advertises (lint, build, test, verify:assets, verify:readme) run only when a human remembers to run them. The retired-model defect F-EXEC-001 is exactly the class of regression a CI smoke test against the live provider surface would have caught, and it shipped undetected.
findings.exploit_or_repro: ls -la .github -> 'No such file or directory'; find . -maxdepth 2 -name 'Dockerfile*' -o -name '*.tf' -> empty.
findings.remediation: Add .github/workflows/ci.yml running on push and pull_request: checkout, setup-node with a pinned Node major and npm cache, npm ci, npm run lint, npm test, npm run build, npm run verify:assets, npm run verify:readme, npm audit --audit-level=moderate.

findings.title: Firebase OAuth requests full Gmail read+send scopes for a dashboard demo
findings.impact: provider.addScope() requests eight scopes including the Google-restricted scope https://mail.google.com/ (full mailbox access) plus gmail.modify, gmail.send and gmail.compose. A compromised or malicious build of this page can read and send the signed-in user's entire mail. Requesting restricted scopes also triggers Google's OAuth verification and, for mail.google.com, a third-party security assessment before the app can be used by anyone outside the test-users list — a launch gate the repository does not address. The scopes exceed what the widget's four Gmail operations need.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of src/lib/firebase.ts:11-18. Not executed — no browser or Google account in the sandbox.
findings.remediation: Reduce to the minimum scopes the widget actually calls (gmail.readonly or gmail.send alone, sheets/ drive.file, docs). Drop https://mail.google.com/ entirely. Document the OAuth verification requirement in the README. Requires a product-owner decision on which operations are in scope.
findings.journey_note: RECONCILED IN PHASE 5: blocks_journey was originally ['J8'] but J8 is classified UNTESTABLE, not BROKEN — the excessive scopes do not break the Workspace code path, they impose a Google-side OAuth verification gate on distribution. blocks_journey is therefore [] and the launch gate is carried by mvp_blocking + requires_human. No score input (severity/grade/confidence) changed, so R_point is unaffected.

findings.title: No coverage instrumentation — test coverage is unmeasurable
findings.impact: vitest.config.ts configures only include and timeouts; there is no coverage provider, no coverage script in package.json, and no coverage threshold. The 57 passing tests cannot be related to the code they cover, so 'tests pass' cannot be read as 'the code is exercised'. Per the scoring contract, unavailable coverage is treated as 0 and caps D2.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Read of vitest.config.ts and package.json scripts — no coverage entry exists.
findings.remediation: Add @vitest/coverage-v8 to devDependencies, a 'test:coverage' script (vitest run --coverage), coverage.include for server.ts, core/, plugins/, src/lib/, and report thresholds in vitest.config.ts.

findings.title: No security response headers; X-Powered-By discloses the stack
findings.impact: The production smoke response carries 'X-Powered-By: Express' and no Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, X-Frame-Options or Strict-Transport-Security. The app renders an agent chat surface and embeds Google OAuth popups, so a missing CSP and frame-busting protection raises clickjacking and injected-content risk.
findings.exploit_or_repro: curl -s -I http://127.0.0.1:3131/ returned the header set above; no security headers present.
findings.remediation: app.disable('x-powered-by') and add helmet (or an explicit header middleware) in server.ts before the routes, with a CSP that permits the googleapis.com origins the Workspace widget calls.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /api/keys/validate is an outbound amplification and key oracle
findings.impact: Each unauthenticated POST triggers one outbound Gemini generation with a caller-supplied key and returns a boolean. There is no rate limit, no per-IP budget and no cost ceiling, so the endpoint is a free outbound-request amplifier and a key-validity oracle for anyone probing stolen keys through this host.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of the route and validateKey(). The 400 guard is covered by tests/api.test.ts:43-50; the outbound call is not rate limited anywhere.
findings.remediation: Rate-limit the key routes (e.g. express-rate-limit, 5 requests / 15 min / IP), require authentication, and return a coarse result that does not distinguish auth failure from network failure.

findings.title: 12 known-vulnerable dependencies; express/qs/body-parser reachable at runtime
findings.impact: npm audit reports {info:0, low:0, moderate:5, high:7, critical:0, total:12}. REACHABILITY ANALYSIS: the seven highs all descend from firebase@12.15.0 -> @firebase/firestore -> @grpc/grpc-js@1.9.16, but the application imports only 'firebase/app' and 'firebase/auth' and contains zero firestore references, so the @grpc/grpc-js server-side advisories are not reachable in the shipped bundle. The remaining browserslist/postcss/nanoid highs are build-time only. The REACHABLE set is express@4.22.2 -> body-parser@1.20.5 -> qs@6.15.2 (moderate, DoS via attacker-controlled isBuffer and array-limit bypass), which sits directly behind express.json() on every route. Fixable in place for all reachable items.
findings.exploit_or_repro: npm audit --json exit code 1 with the metadata above; reachability determined by grepping the import graph for firestore (no matches).
findings.remediation: npm update qs body-parser express postcss nanoid browserslist protobufjs baseline-browser-mapping; pin firebase to a release that lifts @grpc/grpc-js above 1.13.6 or drop the firebase dependency in favour of direct Google Identity Services, since only app+auth are used. Add npm audit --audit-level=moderate to CI.

findings.title: vite.config.ts allowedHosts:true disables the dev host check (DNS rebinding)
findings.impact: Setting allowedHosts: true makes the dev server accept any Host header. Because the API has no authentication and no origin check, a malicious web page a developer visits can resolve an attacker domain to 127.0.0.1 and drive the unauthenticated API — including the destructive purge route — from the developer's own browser session.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading. Not executed — no second host available in the sandbox.
findings.remediation: Replace allowedHosts: true with an explicit allowlist read from an env var (e.g. ALLOWED_DEV_HOSTS), defaulting to localhost/127.0.0.1, and keep the preview-proxy host configurable rather than wildcarded.

findings.title: KeyDeck hard-gates key deployment on one live ping, so any blip means 'Invalid Key'
findings.impact: validateAndSave() only calls /api/keys/save when data.valid is true, and validateKey() normalises every failure — network error, timeout, quota, retired model — to false. A user behind a proxy, with no egress, or hitting a provider outage is told their valid key is invalid and has no way to deploy it except by editing .env and restarting. With F-EXEC-001 present this gate is permanently closed.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading; the normalise-everything-to-false path is directly observed in the npm test stderr trace where a transport failure produced the same false result an invalid key would.
findings.remediation: Distinguish transport failure from authentication failure in validateKey() (return a tri-state), and in KeyDeck allow an explicit 'Save without validating' path so a reachable-provider assumption is never a hard gate.

findings.title: Test suite performs a live outbound network call, making it non-hermetic
findings.impact: tests/orchestrator.test.ts:36 calls orchestrator.validateKey('not-a-real-gemini-key'), which issues a real HTTPS request to generativelanguage.googleapis.com. The suite's outcome therefore depends on network egress and on Google's availability. In this sandbox it passed for the wrong reason — the trace shows ECONNRESET, not a 401 — so the assertion 'invalid key -> false' is satisfied by a transport failure and would also be satisfied if validateKey were rewritten to always return false.
findings.exploit_or_repro: npm test stderr: 'Key Validation Failed TypeError: fetch failed ... host: generativelanguage.googleapis.com port: 443 ... code: ECONNRESET'. Exit code of npm test was still 0.
findings.remediation: Stub global.fetch (or the genai client) inside that test so the ping never leaves the process, and assert the specific provider error shape rather than only the boolean.

findings.title: Seven silent catch blocks swallow UI errors with no log or user feedback
findings.impact: Each 'catch (e) {}' discards the error entirely. Failures in audio playback, clipboard copy, and speech synthesis present as a control that silently does nothing, so a user cannot distinguish a bug from an unsupported browser and support has no signal to work from.
findings.exploit_or_repro: grep -rn 'catch\s*{' over src returned exactly 7 matches, all empty bodies.
findings.remediation: Give each handler a minimal action: console.warn with a labelled prefix plus a user-visible toast/log entry for the interactive ones. Keep silent handling only where the operation is genuinely optional (audio beeps).

findings.title: episodicSummary grows without bound and is re-sent on every request
findings.impact: prune() appends every evicted message's content to episodicSummary with += and nothing ever truncates it, while getContext() emits the whole summary as a system message on every single iteration. A long session therefore grows both server heap and per-request token cost monotonically — the 50-message window bounds the window but not the memory. The constructor's limit parameter (default 12000) is stored in this.limit and never read, so the intended token budget is inert.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading; tests/memory.test.ts asserts pruning behaviour but never asserts a bound on episodicSummary length.
findings.remediation: Cap episodicSummary (character or token budget) with a rolling tail, or replace it with a real summarisation step; wire this.limit into prune() or delete the field. Add a test that drives 500 messages and asserts bounded context length.

findings.title: No request logging, correlation IDs, metrics or error tracking
findings.impact: The entire server emits exactly five console calls, none structured, none with a request identifier. There is no access log, no latency histogram, no error-tracking integration and no way to correlate a browser action with a server-side failure. An operator running REDDY cannot answer 'what did the agent do' or 'why did that request fail' after the fact.
findings.exploit_or_repro: grep -n 'console\.' over server.ts and core/*.ts returned 6 lines total (5 in server.ts, 1 in orchestrator.ts).
findings.remediation: Add a request-logging middleware emitting one structured JSON line per request (method, path, status, duration, request id), propagate the id into engine/orchestrator logs, and add GET /api/health returning process uptime and counters.

findings.title: No container or deploy artifact; no resource bounds or restart policy
findings.impact: find over the repo root returns no Dockerfile, no compose file, no Terraform, no k8s or helm manifests. Deployment is 'npm start' with no process supervisor, no memory ceiling, no declared Node version (no engines field, no .nvmrc, no mise.toml) and no documented rollback. Combined with in-memory state (F-DATA-002) any restart is a silent data reset.
findings.exploit_or_repro: find . -maxdepth 2 -iname 'Dockerfile*' -o -iname 'docker-compose*' -o -iname '*.tf' -> empty; ls mise.toml .nvmrc -> not found.
findings.remediation: Add a multi-stage Dockerfile (pinned node:22-slim, non-root USER, npm ci --omit=dev, dist/ only in the runtime stage), an engines field in package.json, and a documented rollback (previous image tag / previous dist bundle).

findings.title: No health endpoint; SPA catch-all answers unknown /api paths with 200 HTML
findings.impact: GET /api/health returned HTTP 200 in the production smoke test because app.get('*') at server.ts:298 serves dist/index.html for every unmatched path, including unmatched API paths. A load balancer or orchestrator probing /api/health gets a false-positive healthy signal, and any mistyped API call receives 200 text/html instead of a JSON 404 — which breaks every client that expects JSON and hides integration errors.
findings.exploit_or_repro: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3131/api/health -> 200 on the built production server.
findings.remediation: Register GET /api/health before the catch-all returning JSON {status, uptime, version}, and add an /api/* 404 handler that returns JSON before the SPA fallback so unknown API routes never return HTML.

findings.title: Knowledge IDs come from Math.random and DELETE is unauthenticated
findings.impact: Identifiers are Math.random().toString(36).substring(7) — roughly 6-8 base36 characters from a non-cryptographic, non-seeded PRNG. Collisions silently overwrite an existing entry in the Map, and because DELETE /api/knowledge/:id has no authentication and returns 200 even for unknown ids, the whole vault is enumerable and destructible by any client that can reach the port.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of the id generation and the delete route; tests/api.test.ts covers the happy path only.
findings.remediation: Use crypto.randomUUID() for identifiers, return 404 from DELETE when the id is absent, and gate the route behind the auth middleware from F-SEC-002.

findings.title: All server state is process memory; a restart silently destroys it
findings.impact: Sessions, session protocols, the knowledge vault, injected skills and the telemetry buffer are four in-process Maps/arrays with no write-behind. A deploy, crash or OOM loses every knowledge entry the operator curated, with no warning and no export path. The README discloses this and the Open engineering questions section lists persistence as the first backlog item, so it is a known, accepted MVP constraint rather than a hidden defect.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of the state declarations; the production smoke test's task history contained only the 15 boot-seeded records.
findings.remediation: Persist the knowledge vault first (highest value, smallest volume) to a JSON file or SQLite with an atomic write, then sessions. Add an export route so operators can evacuate state before a restart.

findings.title: God components: App.tsx 1186 LOC and WorkspaceWidget.tsx 845 LOC
findings.impact: src/App.tsx mixes the boot screen, custom cursor, Web Audio alarms, chat transport, settings panel, purge console and log rendering in one 1186-line component. src/components/WorkspaceWidget.tsx carries Sheets, Gmail and Docs clients, OAuth token state and all rendering in 845 lines. Neither can be unit tested in isolation — which is why the 57 tests cover core/ and the API but no component at all.
findings.exploit_or_repro: wc -l over src core plugins server.ts scripts tests: App.tsx 1186, WorkspaceWidget.tsx 845, AnimatedVectorIcons.tsx 602.
findings.remediation: Extract a useChat/usePurgeSettings hook pair and a ChatTerminal component from App.tsx; split WorkspaceWidget into SheetsPanel, GmailPanel and DocsPanel over a shared useGoogleToken hook.

findings.title: No privacy policy despite Gmail scopes and localStorage chat mirroring
findings.impact: The product reads and sends the user's email and mirrors the full chat log plus the system instruction into browser localStorage, yet the repository ships no privacy policy, no data-retention statement and no data-subject-deletion path. Requesting restricted Gmail scopes without a published policy is also a Google OAuth verification blocker.
findings.exploit_or_repro: git ls-files shows no privacy/policy document; the scopes and localStorage keys were read directly.
findings.remediation: Publish a privacy policy covering the OAuth scopes, the localStorage keys, the server-side in-memory retention and the deletion story; add a 'Clear local data' control to the UI. Requires an owner decision.

findings.title: Firebase web API key committed (public-by-design, redacted in all outputs)
findings.impact: The mandatory signature scan found the value [REDACTED:GENERIC:****Guus:len=39:sha256=7bd73af1] at firebase-applet-config.json:4, plus an oAuthClientId. Firebase Web SDK configuration is public by design and is shipped to every browser, and the README states this explicitly, so this is not a credential leak. The residual risk is that the project's HTTP-referrer restrictions in the Firebase console cannot be verified from the repository; without them the project's Firebase Auth quota is abusable by any site.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Node signature scanner over every tracked file at HEAD; 2 hits total, both reported here in redacted form. No liveness test was performed and none will be.
findings.remediation: Leave the file committed (it must reach the browser) but document in the README that the Firebase console must restrict the key by HTTP referrer, and enable Firebase App Check for Auth.

findings.title: Blocking fs I/O in request handlers and no timeout on the provider call
findings.impact: scanDirectory uses readdirSync/statSync/readFileSync and the purge route uses readFileSync/writeFileSync synchronously inside the request path, so one audit or purge call stalls the single-threaded event loop for every other client. Separately, models.generateContent is called with no AbortSignal and no timeout, so a hung provider holds the request open indefinitely and the browser sees no error.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Static reading of the scanner and the provider call; no abort/timeout option is passed anywhere in core/orchestrator.ts.
findings.remediation: Convert the purge scanner and rewrite to fs.promises, and pass an AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) (or the genai SDK's httpOptions timeout) to generateContent and validateKey.

findings.title: Frontend ships as one 943.84 kB chunk; Vite warns above 500 kB
findings.impact: vite build emits dist/assets/index-BkWU8Cg-.js at 943.84 kB (268.67 kB gzip) and prints the chunk-size warning. recharts, motion, firebase and lucide-react all land in the initial bundle, so first paint on a cold cache pays for the whole dashboard including widgets the user may never open.
findings.exploit_or_repro: npm run build output: 'dist/assets/index-BkWU8Cg-.js 943.84 kB | gzip: 268.67 kB' plus the >500 kB advisory.
findings.remediation: React.lazy the heavy widgets (WorkspaceWidget, SunoWidget, AnimatedVectorIcons) and add build.rollupOptions.output.manualChunks for recharts/motion/firebase.

findings.title: Dead code: inert MemoryVault.limit field and an empty settings branch
findings.impact: MemoryVault stores this.limit = limit (default 12000) and never reads it, so the documented token budget is fictional. In server.ts the else branch of the /api/chat session lookup binds vault and currentProtocol, then contains only the comment 'Logic to update existing vault system prompt could be added here' — meaning a protocol changed via POST /api/settings does not reach an already-created session's pinned system prompt, contradicting the README's claim that updateSystemPrompt is 'how the settings API changes behavior mid-session'.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Direct reading of both sites; MemoryVault.updateSystemPrompt exists at core/memory.ts:27-33 and is only called from POST /api/settings, never from the chat path.
findings.remediation: Either call vault.updateSystemPrompt(currentProtocol) in that branch or delete the branch; wire this.limit into prune() or remove the field and its constructor parameter.

findings.title: Shipped identity is placeholder: package name react-example, title 'My Google AI Studio App'
findings.impact: package.json declares name 'react-example' at version 0.0.0 and index.html's <title> is 'My Google AI Studio App', so the browser tab and every crash report say the scaffold name rather than REDDY Agent. A new contributor cloning the repo sees a name that contradicts the 471-line README.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Direct read of both files.
findings.remediation: Set package.json name to 'reddy-agent' with a real version, and change the index.html title to 'REDDY Agent'.

findings.title: Telemetry buffer boots with 15 fabricated records shown in the live chart
findings.impact: taskHistory is seeded at boot with 15 records whose success flags and latencies come from Math.random(). GET /api/tasks/history returns them indistinguishably from real executions, and TaskTracker renders them into the success-ratio and average-latency figures — so the dashboard's headline numbers are partly invented until 15 real requests arrive. The README discloses the seeding and the Open engineering questions section asks whether they should be visually distinguished.
findings.exploit_or_repro: Direct read of the seeding code; the production smoke test returned 'Task Execution #0' as the first history record on a fresh boot.
findings.remediation: Add a 'seeded': true flag to the synthetic records and have TaskTracker render them in a muted series, or drop the seeding entirely and show an empty-state message.
